name: Mars Aerostat
operator: CNES and IKI (France, USSR then Russia)
short_status: Terminated in 1995 over money, with hardware built and tested on Earth. No balloon has ever been released at Mars; only its relay receiver flew, on Mars Observer in 1992 and Mars Global Surveyor in 1996.
tagline: CNES and IKI (France, USSR then Russia) · Multinational · Aircraft · 1986 · The losing decade Cancelled
stats: balloons ever released into the atmosphere of Mars
distance one balloon was expected to cover in about ten day-night cycles
piece of it that flew: the Mars Balloon Relay, on two NASA orbiters

facts.label: What it was
facts.value: A balloon (aerostat in the Russian and French usage) to be deployed and inflated during the descent of an entry capsule at Mars, then left to drift. The division of labour was fixed early: the French would supply the balloon system, the Soviets the gondola and the delivery to Mars. Neither part ever flew.

facts.label: Where the idea came from
facts.value: A JPL team led by Viktor Kerzhanovich, who had worked on the Venus balloons himself, records that the first practical concept for a balloon mission in the atmosphere of Mars was initiated in April 1986 by French and Soviet researchers, on the strength of the first planetary balloon mission, the Venus Vega balloons of 1985, and that the Vega heritage significantly influenced the Mars Aerostat approach, specifically in how the balloon was to be deployed. The French archive nirgal.net puts the Vega flight at about two days at a nearly constant altitude near 54 km, and credits the idea of a wind-borne planetary balloon principally to Jacques Blamont.

facts.label: Programme span
facts.value: Kerzhanovich's team date the effort as the Russian-French Mars Aerostat Project, 1988 to 1995. Anatoly Zak's reconstruction of the Russian side starts earlier: in May 1987 NPO Lavochkin issued documentation for the MS-92 complex (manufacturing index M1), a pair of spacecraft for 1992 each carrying a 240 kg rover, a 120 kg balloon and a 55 kg penetrator. By December 1987 the launch had slipped to 1994, the penetrator was dropped, and France had taken on what Zak describes as a giant sausage-shaped balloon of 6,000 cubic metres.

facts.label: The first design
facts.value: Two cells. A spherical helium balloon on top, able on its own to hold the gondola and guiderope off the ground, and below it an oval solar Montgolfiere with a dark envelope and an opening that let Martian air circulate. Sunlight was to heat the lower cell, and the assembly would lift once the air inside was about 55 degrees hotter than the air outside. Nirgal.net gives this configuration a total of 33 kg, of which 17 kg was envelope, 2 kg helium and 14 kg science gondola, a life of about ten days set by battery discharge, and roughly 500 km covered per day at mid-latitudes. A later refinement added valves to dump hot air so the balloon could be made to stay down or land in daylight.

facts.label: The design it became
facts.value: Kerry Nock's JPL team record that the concept eventually evolved into a 6-micron thick mylar balloon which would be overpressure during the day, descending to the surface during the night. Nirgal.net describes that version as a single translucent helium cylinder of 6,000 cubic metres, 45 m tall and 12 m across, inflated over about four minutes through special nozzles so the gas jet could not tear the film. English retellings, including Andrew LePage's and Global Aerospace Corporation's, instead describe a 20 m (66 ft) two-part Mylar balloon with helium on top and Martian air below, which is the earlier configuration.

facts.label: The published numbers, and how far apart they sit
facts.value: The volume most often quoted, 5,500 cubic metres, together with a daytime ceiling of 2 to 4 km above the reference level, a total floating mass of 65.4 kg, a 15 kg gondola and a 13.5 kg guide rope, traces to the CNES simulator paper: A. Vargas, C. Tarrieu, J.-P. Lepage, P. Mauroy and C. Sirmain, Mars balloon simulator, Acta Astronautica 26, 8-10, pp. 697-706, 1992. We verified that citation but could not read the paywalled text, so those figures are reported here at second hand. They disagree with the 6,000 cubic metres given by Zak and by nirgal.net, and with nirgal's cruise description of a late-morning climb to about 6,000 m. The masses move as much as the volume: Zak's chronology has the gondola at 48 kg in the 1988 preliminary design, 57.5 kg in the September 1989 revision and the balloon itself at 200 kg, nirgal gives 60 kg for the later cylinder split evenly between balloon and payload, and popular accounts describe a 4 kg camera package and a 4 kg snake. These are successive designs and different accountings rather than competing measurements of one object.

facts.label: Flight profile as intended
facts.value: Global Aerospace Corporation, whose staff worked on the JPL balloon studies that followed, set out the cycle: by day the sun-heated balloon would rise to between 2 and 4 km and travel hundreds of kilometres on the Martian winds while a gondola camera photographed the ground; at nightfall the balloon would sink until the guiderope reached the surface, where instruments on it would take measurements; the next morning it would rise again. About ten such cycles were expected before enough helium had leaked away to stop the balloon ascending, covering roughly 1,500 km in all. The ten-day mission length is the same figure the CNES and JPL papers give. The distance is not: that roughly 1,500 km rests on this one uncited page, and it sits awkwardly beside nirgal.net's roughly 500 km a day for the earlier two-cell design, which over ten days would be nearer 5,000 km. No primary paper we could open gives a traverse total at all.

facts.label: The guiderope, or SNAKE
facts.value: Kerzhanovich's team credit The Planetary Society with developing the concept of the snake or guiderope, which enabled the balloon to tolerate diurnal descents to the surface as the balloon cooled at night and permitted a mission duration of about 10 days as well as in situ surface data. Nock's team describe the mechanism: at night the balloon would rest on the surface on a guiderope or landing snake suspended from the gondola, and the mass of the landing snake on the surface relieved negative buoyancy so that the gondola did not touch the ground.

facts.label: How the SNAKE was built
facts.value: A chain of overlapping cones. Charlene Anderson of The Planetary Society described it as a nested Dixie cup design that gives the SNAKE the flexibility to serve as a self-ballasting guide-rope for the balloon, as well as the rigidity to avoid snagging and to protect its internal instruments. It was painted fluorescent orange for the field tests and carried instruments to measure its speed under the balloon and the friction between it and the ground. Nirgal.net describes the flight article as interconnected elements holding batteries, heaters, the data transmission system, science instruments and an antenna.

facts.label: The Mojave tests, 1990
facts.value: Through the summer and into the early autumn of 1990 the balloon and guiderope were tested in California: the SNAKE dragged behind a truck first, then flown beneath a CNES balloon over the dunes of Palen Dry Lake, with the team working out of Indio, the hardpan of Coyote Dry Lake and the basalt of the Pisgah lava flows. The team was CNES scientists and technicians, observers from the Babakin Center, scientists from the Space Research Institute of the Soviet Academy of Sciences, JPL engineers, students from Arizona, Utah State, UCLA and Caltech, and Planetary Society volunteers. Anderson's report: the balloon flew flawlessly in both heavy and light winds, and the SNAKE slithered obliviously over sand, hardpan and lava boulders.

facts.label: What the Society then did with it
facts.value: Anderson wrote that The Planetary Society has fulfilled its initial obligation: the design of a guide-rope to enable low-altitude flight over martian terrain and to carry instruments to the surface, and that the Society had transferred all of its data and designs to CNES for incorporation into the Soviet Mars '94 mission. The cover of that issue called the balloon and its SNAKE an intrinsic and official part of the Soviet Mars '94 mission.

facts.label: The drop tests
facts.value: Nock's team record that the Mars '96 Martian Aerostat system encountered difficulties during the two high altitude drop-and-deploy tests, and that the lessons learned identified key stability problems, which is why their own later design hung the balloon from the parachute and put the inflation hardware at its base, even though a top-down inflation like those of Vega and Mars '96 had been highly desired. On the Russian side a parachute system for these trials was developed and reported by R. S. Kremnev, K. M. Pichkhadze, V. M. Linkin, V. V. Kerzhanovich and colleagues, Balloon experiments in the Earth's stratosphere within the Mars-96 project, Advances in Space Research 17, 9, pp. 77-80, 1996. We verified the citation but could not read the paywalled text.

facts.label: The relay that flew
facts.value: The Mars Balloon Relay (MBR), principal investigator Jacques Blamont, was a 6.8 kg UHF package on NASA's Mars Observer drawing 12.5 W. In orbit it would transmit a continuous 437 MHz beacon at the surface; when a station or the balloon saw the signal cross a threshold it would answer on 401 or 405 MHz; the MBR would demodulate, measure the Doppler shift for localisation and balloon tracking, and pass everything into the memory buffer of the Mars Observer Camera. Two contacts a day, each about 11 minutes, at 2 a.m. and 2 p.m. local time, through a rigidly mounted quadrifilar helix with a 65 degree conical pattern.

facts.label: What the relay was for
facts.value: NASA's catalogue states that the MBR was planned to augment the return of data from the penetrators and surface stations of the Russian Mars '94 mission and from penetrators, surface stations, a rover, and a balloon from the Mars '96 mission. Mars Observer fell silent on 22 August 1993 UTC (still 21 August in Pasadena), less than three days before orbit insertion, and no data were returned. The experiment was rebuilt for Mars Global Surveyor as the Mars Relay: 10.5 kg, an 86 cm quadrifilar helix fibreglass mast, 437.1 MHz at 1.3 W down, 401.5 and 405.6 MHz up, again buffering through the camera.

facts.label: What the relay actually carried
facts.value: Not balloons. Emily Lakdawalla, reporting the Mars Orbiter Camera team's end-of-mission accounting, records that the Mars Relay wound up relaying data not from Mars balloons but instead from two rovers, and that a total of 7,680 megabits of rover data came through the Mars Relay on MOC.

facts.label: What flew instead
facts.value: Mars-96 launched on 16 November 1996 carrying an orbiter, two small autonomous surface stations and two penetrators. The Institute of Space Research project description edited by A. V. Zakharov, published in 1996, lists exactly those elements and no aerostat and no rover. The spacecraft never left Earth orbit.

timeline: French and Soviet researchers begin work on what Kerzhanovich's team call the first practical concept for a balloon mission in the atmosphere of Mars, ten months after the two Vega balloons flew in the atmosphere of Venus.
NPO Lavochkin issues documentation for the MS-92 complex, index M1: two spacecraft to launch in 1992, each carrying a 240 kg rover, a 120 kg balloon and a 55 kg penetrating probe.

The technical proposal is ready but the launch moves to 1994 and the penetrator is dropped. France takes on the balloon: 6,000 cubic metres, instruments in an aerial gondola and more instruments dragged along the surface on a rope.

With the Soviet space budget being trimmed, the revised preliminary design drops the rover. The balloon survives the cut, now with a 57.5 kg gondola, alongside 20 kg meteorological landers and a 60 kg penetrator.

Field tests in the Mojave. The SNAKE is dragged behind a truck, then flown under a CNES balloon over Palen Dry Lake, Coyote Dry Lake and the Pisgah lava flows by a team of French, Soviet and American engineers and Planetary Society volunteers. The Society hands its data and designs to CNES.
Mars Observer launches carrying the Mars Balloon Relay, the receiver built under Jacques Blamont to talk to the Russian landers and to the balloon.

Nock's team date the damage: as early as 1992 the joint programme was feeling the effects of the collapse of the Soviet Union, and the immediate impact was a slip of the launch to at least 1996. Zak dates the same damage a year earlier: with the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 the project lost its second spacecraft, and France withdrew from it over overspending on its own share.
Mars Observer falls silent less than three days before orbit insertion (21 August in California). The Mars Balloon Relay returns nothing. The instrument is later rebuilt for Mars Global Surveyor.
C. Tarrieu presents a status paper at the IAF congress in Graz. Its title records where the balloon had moved to: Status of the Mars 96 Aerostat Development.

It becomes clear the mission must slip again, this time to 1998. That would put the balloon in the northern hemisphere in winter, with surface winds above 30 m/s, fast enough to destroy a balloon whose snake was dragging on the ground. The French continue a scaled-back development with real successes and some nagging balloon deployment failures.

The end. Kerzhanovich's team write that due to budget problems the Russian-French development was terminated in 1995. Nock's team give the cause as a combination of programmatic and related technical problems. Nirgal.net instead follows the mission slot, which moved to a Mars-98 that was itself cancelled after Mars-96 failed.

Mars-96 launches with an orbiter, two small stations and two penetrators, and no balloon. The Blok D-2 stage fails its second burn and the spacecraft re-enters. Nine days earlier Mars Global Surveyor had left Earth carrying the rebuilt relay, which would spend its working life listening to rovers.

images.caption: The Mars balloon in flight during the 1990 desert tests: the long envelope high against a blue sky and broken cloud, the small gondola hanging below it, and the line running down to the desert floor where the guiderope has drawn a track across a dune. The Society's timeline entry for 1990 reads: Planetary Society members support desert testing of the Mars Balloon, slated to fly on the Soviet Mars '96 mission.
images.credit: The Planetary Society (the page names no photographer; the cover photograph of the same test campaign is credited in the magazine to Charlene M. Anderson)

images.caption: The cover of The Planetary Report volume XI number 1, January and February 1991, headlined The Mars Balloon: It Works!, carrying a photograph of the balloon aloft over the Mojave with its guiderope trailing to the ground. The cover note inside reads that the French-built Mars Balloon, equipped with the SNAKE guide-rope designed by The Planetary Society, is an intrinsic and official part of the Soviet Mars '94 mission, that during tests in California's Mojave Desert we proved that our design works, and that the photograph is by Charlene M. Anderson.
images.credit: The Planetary Society; cover photograph by Charlene M. Anderson

images.caption: A CNES sequence drawing headed AEROSTAT LAUNCHING, tracking the balloon from aerodynamic braking and parachute descent through parachute and balloon separation, deployment and balloon filling, first landing and balloon mission starting, with the rover's separate trajectory dotted across the same panel. The balloon is drawn in two parts, a pale upper cell over a dark lower one, and the guiderope reaches the ground at every stage after the first landing. Drew Ex Machina's caption reads: An early concept from 1988 for the deployment of the French balloon for the Mars 1994 mission. Since then, the rover has been replaced with penetrators.
images.credit: CNES, as credited by Drew Ex Machina; the drawing is signed david ducros

images.caption: A CNES painting of the balloon's daily cycle on Mars, the same envelope drawn several times across one panel: high in daylight at the left and right, sinking as the light fails, and resting at night in the middle of the picture with its guiderope lying on the ground under a black sky. Drew Ex Machina's caption reads: Depiction of the daily cycle of the French-made balloon for the Mars 1994 mission.
images.credit: CNES / David Ducros, as credited by Drew Ex Machina

images.caption: Mars Global Surveyor standing in a clean room before its 1996 launch, gold thermal blankets over the bus, technicians working at it, and a white arrow with the words Mars Relay pointing at the pale cylindrical mast on the top deck. The MSSS page describes that mast as a quadrifilar helix fibreglass antenna approximately 80 cm tall and 10 cm in diameter.
